profile.context: Runs a 20-to-50 person machine or job shop with no dedicated training or documentation department.
profile.mindset: Pragmatic, focused on machine uptime, scrap reduction, safety, and margin protection.
profile.tech_comfort: Moderate; values low-friction tools with clear ROI that do not pull machinists off production for hours of data entry.

pain_points: Single point of failure: veteran machinists hold decades of undocumented fixes, machine quirks, and setup tweaks in their heads.
Blind spots: doesn't know which critical steps are missing from official manuals and work instructions until after the veteran leaves.
Costly onboarding: new hires take months to ramp up, produce scrap on finicky lines, or require expensive OEM service calls.
Dead documentation: existing SOPs and OEM manuals are outdated or omit the 2-to-5 'secret steps' required to actually run the part.
Data security concerns: bound by OEM confidentiality or ITAR restrictions, preventing use of generic consumer tools.
goals: Capture institutional knowledge before a retiring employee's departure date without disrupting floor production.
Identify gaps between written work instructions/manuals and how jobs are actually run on the floor.
Understand where knowledge is covered and where critical gaps remain across machines, part numbers, and jobs.
Reduce time-to-productivity and scrap rates for incoming apprentices.

profile.context: 20+ years of experience as a machinist, tool and die maker, or industrial mechanic; preparing to retire.
profile.mindset: Proud of their craft and hard-won expertise; wants to leave a lasting legacy and keep the shop succeeding, but dislikes bureaucracy and desk work.
profile.tech_comfort: Prefers hands-on work over keyboards and paperwork.

pain_points: Doesn't want to spend their final months typing up binders of SOPs at a desk.
Unconscious competence: decades of intuition make critical checks (e.g., shimming a fixture, listening for spindle chatter) feel too 'obvious' to mention unprompted.
Skepticism of being misrepresented: worried someone else will document a complex setup inaccurately, causing scrap or safety hazards.
Emotional friction: wants their knowledge respected and credited as mentorship/legacy rather than feeling like a replacement exercise.
goals: Pass down decades of practical know-how naturally without tedious writing or administrative overhead.
Surface the subtle 'secret steps' and sensory cues they perform by habit.
Ensure any documentation created from their expertise is accurate and safe.
Be recognized and remembered as the expert teaching the next generation.

profile.context: Newly hired machinist or apprentice learning to set up, operate, and troubleshoot specific machines and parts.
profile.mindset: Eager to perform well and avoid costly mistakes or scrap, but hesitant to constantly interrupt busy senior staff with repetitive questions.
profile.tech_comfort: High digital literacy; expects fast, clear, and accessible guidance right where the work happens.

pain_points: Written work instructions skip the real-world adjustments needed to make a part run in tolerance.
Intimidation and bottlenecks: senior operators are busy or already retired, leaving no one to ask when a setup goes wrong.
Hostile environment for traditional docs: wearing gloves, surrounded by shop noise, and working at the machine where binders and long manuals are impractical.
Fear of bad advice: an inaccurate offset or maintenance step can ruin a part, break a tool, or cause an injury.
goals: Follow clear instructions that include both official specs and the veteran's real-world tips and warnings.
Get immediate, trustworthy answers to troubleshooting questions while at the machine.
Understand exactly how the veteran approaches a tricky step, including what to look, listen, or feel for.
Ramp up to independent operation faster with fewer mistakes.
